mainEntity.name: Christ Driving The Moneychangers From The Temple
mainEntity.description:
Prolific sculptor, typographer and printmaker Eric Gill was born in Sussex and initially trained to be an architect, abandoning his studies in 1903 and eventually establishing himself as a sculptor. Known for his precise linear simplicity, Gill was associated with the modernist direct carving movement, which encouraged a return to skills favoured in the Middle Ages. He became the subject of posthumous scandal when a 1989 biography revealed his sexual abuse of his daughters.

In 1914 Gill was commissioned to create the Stations of the Cross for Westminster Cathedral. While he was working on these, the University’s Vice-Chancellor Michael Sadler approached him about a war memorial for Leeds, and commissioned him in 1917. Gill revived a proposal that the London County Council had rejected for its own war memorial – a freestanding bronze of Jesus and the moneychangers – and suggested a stone frieze for Leeds, with Christ expelling a group of moneychangers from the temple, some of them in contemporary dress.

Gill’s relief was carved in five sections and was dedicated by the Bishop of Ripon on 1 June 1923, in its prominent original site on the wall beneath the Great Hall. It represents the Bible story in which Christ violently expels traders and moneychangers from a temple. This moralising subject was popular in European art, but it was very different from the soldiers or mourning angels expected of a 20th-century war memorial, and it caused immediate comment. The Yorkshire Post described it as a ‘curious monument which... promises to create much controversy’, and other local press called it ‘bizarre’, ‘puzzling’, ‘strange’ and ‘not appropriate’. Gill enjoyed the controversy and published his own defence of the work, and others, including JRR Tolkien, rallied to defend it.

Gill held intensely religious, anti-industrial beliefs and thought modern warfare was driven by monetary gain. Some believed he was implying that Leeds merchants had profited from the war. For Sadler, however, the subject affirmed the Allies’ use of force as justifiable. Like Christ, they used violence as the last resort in a righteous cause. For Sadler, the frieze presented the war as an ethical rather than a military triumph, and he steadfastly championed it as ‘one of the finest things in modern art’, adding ‘the carving will tell its own tale’. In recent times, the frieze has been criticised for what can be read as an antisemitic trope that associates money changing with Jewish people.

The weather took its toll on the work and ivy was allowed to grow over it, until in 1961 it was moved indoors to its current location in the foyer of the Michael Sadler Building.

This work was conserved in 2018 thanks to the Henry Moore Foundation, the Friends of University Art and Music (Leeds) and Leeds Arts Fund.
